corrected_value.title: Racial Disparities in Autism Identification in the United States During 2014
corrected_value.title_o: Racial Disparities in Autism Identification in the United States During 2014

decisions.quote:
Claim Summary

The claim selected for replication in Travers & Krezmien (2018) is that, compared to California,
the odds ratio of autism identification was lower in the state of Ohio. This reflects the following
statement from the paper's abstract: "Between-state analyses revealed White students and
minority students in most states were underidentified compared to White students with autism in
California."
decisions.location: Claim Summary, p. 2, lines 34-40 (and Citation, p. 6, lines 195-198)
decisions.reason: Both the shipped row (input_row_index 2575) and blind target 0 identify the same focal original study: Travers & Krezmien (2018), 'Racial Disparities in Autism Identification in the United States During 2014', Exceptional Children, 84(4):403-419. The conflicting_dois flag arose only because the primary report's reference list prints a truncated DOI ('doi:10.1177/001440291877133', missing the final digit '7'), which the blind coding copied verbatim while the shipped record holds the complete canonical DOI ('10.1177/0014402918771337').

decisions.quote:
The result suggests that, compared to California, Ohio is significantly less likely to identify
students with autism. Ohio’s odds ratio of autism identification is 0.91, with a 95%
confidence interval equal to [0.90, 0.93], i.e., it lies entirely below 1.0. The odds ratio is
statistically significant at the 5% level (p = 0.000). Thus, this replication of the claim was
successful according to the SCORE criteria.
decisions.reason: With the identity of the tested original (Travers & Krezmien, 2018) resolved and the study type confirmed as a replication using 2017 data, the authors state an explicit overall verdict that the replication of the focal claim (lower odds of autism identification in Ohio compared to California, OR = 0.91, 95% CI [0.90, 0.93], p = 0.000) was successful according to the SCORE criteria. Both shipped and blind codings agree on 'successful'.

decisions.quote:
Deviations from the Original Study

   1. Although the data sources are the same (the IDEA Data and the Digest of Education
       Statistics), the original study relied on data from 2014, while the replication study uses data
       from 2017.
decisions.location: Deviations from the Original Study, p. 6, lines 181-185
decisions.reason: The study re-tests a published claim from Travers & Krezmien (2018) using a new sample from a different year (2017 IDEA and Digest of Education Statistics data rather than the 2014 data analyzed in the original study). Under the codebook, re-testing a previously published finding using a different sample is a 'replication'. Both shipped and blind codings agree.
